title: Orsen and the Undertow
premise: Yara Iversen has spent seven years writing postcards to a house that no longer exists, addressed to the person they loved and failed to save from the fire that took the old harbor district. When demolition crews schedule the ruin's final teardown, a box of returned letters surfaces behind a wardrobe in Yara's rented room—letters written by the other hand, never delivered, revealing that the silence ran both ways. As the demolition date closes in, Yara must finally translate the sentence they have circled for years: what actually happened the night of the fire, and who they became by walking away. The book ends with Yara standing at the rubble line on demolition morning, reading the last undelivered letter aloud to the empty lot—not forgiven, but no longer invisible.
about_author: O. M. Delacroix is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing undeliverable mail from coastal towns. They write quietly devastating fiction about people who communicate everything except the thing that matters.

chapters.title: Poste Restante
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, Yara's POV. We meet Yara at their ritual: writing a postcard to an address that burned down seven years ago, then filing it unmailed. The chapter establishes the rhythm of almost-saying-it and the approaching demolition notice pinned to the wall. Emotional beat: comfortable avoidance beginning to itch.

chapters.title: The Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Moving furniture to paint over water damage, Yara finds a box wedged behind the wardrobe: forty-one letters, all addressed to them, all returned undelivered—written by Noor, the person they thought had stopped writing first. Emotional beat: vertigo; the ground truth of seven years cracks open.

chapters.title: What the Fire Took, Alphabetically
chapters.summary: Yara reads the early letters, which are light, funny, forgiving. Flashbacks braid in: the harbor district, the friendship that was more than friendship, the night of the fire told only in fragments Yara can bear. Emotional beat: tenderness curdling into dread as the letters approach the fire's date.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, with interludes from Noor's letters. One letter contains a single sentence in their private invented language—the one they built as children—and it is the accusation or absolution Yara cannot parse. They begin hunting for the key: an old notebook, a dictionary they made together. Emotional beat: obsessive hope.

chapters.title: Demolition Date
chapters.summary: Yara visits the condemned house, now fenced and tagged, and encounters Petra, a salvage worker cataloguing what remains of the district for a memory archive. Petra becomes the first person in years Yara speaks to about anything real. Emotional beat: cautious re-entry into the world; belonging offered and half-refused.

chapters.title: Letters to the Living
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Spurred by the box, Yara writes actual letters—to a estranged sister, to Petra, even to the demolition company asking for one hour on-site. Most go unanswered; the sister replies with three cold lines. Emotional beat: the cost of reaching out made concrete; survival-by-silence examined.

chapters.title: The Key Was Always Yours
chapters.summary: Yara finds the childhood cipher notebook in a storage unit their sister kept, discovering the code's final page was completed after the fire—in Noor's handwriting alone. The translated sentence begins to assemble itself, word by word, each word worse than the last. Emotional beat: rising dread; the price of survival coming due.

chapters.title: Undertow
chapters.summary: Climax approaches. Yara deciphers the full sentence: not blame, but a confession—Noor set the fire accidentally and wrote to say so, then stopped when every letter returned. Yara realizes their own returned postcards may have convinced Noor they were dead or gone. Emotional beat: devastation inverted; guilt reframed as shared drowning.

chapters.title: One Hour On-Site
chapters.summary: Climax. The demolition company grants Yara's request. Inside the gutted house, Yara finds evidence Noor survived the fire and left town—alive, maybe findable—with hours left before the walls come down. Yara must choose between digging for a forwarding address or standing witness to the destruction. Emotional beat: panic, decision, agency reclaimed.

chapters.title: Read Aloud to an Empty Lot
chapters.summary: Resolution, Yara's POV. Demolition morning: Yara stands at the fence and reads Noor's final letter aloud as the machines arrive, then mails a new postcard—a real address this time, found in the salvage archive Petra helped search. Whether it arrives is left open. Emotional beat: grief integrated; visibility chosen; belonging begun rather than found.
